baked_goods.intro: This easy cannabis %{name} recipe uses %{base_fat} for a consistent, potent infusion that bakes beautifully at %{cook_temp}. Baked goods are one of the most popular ways to enjoy edibles because the fat binds perfectly with THC. Follow our step-by-step guide to get reliable dosing every time.
dosing_tips: New to edibles? Start with about 5 mg of THC, a fraction of one serving, and wait 2 hours before eating more.
Mix your %{base_fat} thoroughly into the batter to ensure even distribution of THC across every piece.
Use our calculator to determine the total milligrams in your %{base_fat}, then divide by the number of portions you plan to cut.
Remember that baked goods can take 45-90 minutes to take effect because they must be digested first.
common_mistakes: Overbaking. Bake at the temperature in the recipe and start checking a few minutes before the time it gives; extra minutes dry it out.
Skipping decarboxylation before infusing your fat is the most common beginner mistake and will result in weak or inactive edibles.
Not mixing the %{base_fat} evenly into the batter leads to hot spots where one piece is extremely potent and another has almost nothing.
Opening the oven door frequently causes temperature fluctuations that can affect both the bake and cannabinoid preservation.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Swap %{base_fat} for cannabis-infused coconut oil for a dairy-free version that still binds THC effectively.
Add a teaspoon of sunflower lecithin to your batter to help the infused fat mix in evenly, so every piece gets the same dose.
Try using a mix of CBD and THC-infused fat for a more balanced, less intoxicating effect that is great for daytime use.

faq.q: Can I use cannabis flower directly in the batter instead of infused fat?
faq.a: Technically yes, but it is not recommended. Raw flower must be decarboxylated first, and even then it creates a gritty texture and uneven dosing. Infusing your %{base_fat} first gives a much smoother result and more reliable potency.

faq.q: How do I know if my oven temperature is accurate?
faq.a: Oven thermostats can be off by 25 degrees or more. Use an oven thermometer to verify the actual temperature matches %{cook_temp}. This matters because excessive heat degrades THC while too-low temperatures may underbake your goods.

faq.q: Will my %{name} smell like cannabis while baking?
faq.a: Yes, there will be a noticeable cannabis aroma while baking, especially in the first 15-20 minutes. Using properly infused and strained %{base_fat} reduces the smell compared to adding flower directly. Good ventilation helps.

faq.q: How long do cannabis baked goods stay potent?
faq.a: Longer than they stay fresh. THC breaks down slowly with heat, light and air, so the food goes stale or spoils first. Keep them sealed and cool, follow the storage note for this recipe, and freeze what you won't eat soon.

faq.q: Can I adjust the dosage after baking?
faq.a: You cannot reduce the dosage once baked, but you can cut smaller pieces. This is why accurate calculation before baking is essential. Use our dosage calculator to plan your total THC content and number of servings before you start.

frozen.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe combines %{base_fat} with frozen dessert techniques for a refreshing, perfectly dosed treat. Frozen edibles are ideal for warm weather and offer a discreet, delicious way to consume cannabis. The cold temperatures help preserve cannabinoids while delivering a smooth experience.
dosing_tips: Frozen desserts are easy to over-consume because they taste so good and the cold masks the cannabis flavor. Stick to one measured portion.
Blend your %{base_fat} into the liquid base thoroughly before freezing to prevent THC from separating or settling unevenly.
Use exact measuring tools to portion your mixture before it sets, so every scoop or bar carries the same dose.
Frozen treats go down easily, so serve one portion at a time and wait 2 hours before having more.
common_mistakes: Not emulsifying the %{base_fat} properly causes it to separate during freezing, leaving some portions with no THC and others with too much.
Forgetting to churn or stir periodically during freezing creates ice crystals and uneven texture that also affects dose distribution.
Using too much cannabis fat can throw off the fat ratio of your recipe, resulting in a greasy texture instead of a creamy one.
Serving directly from the freezer without letting it temper for 5-10 minutes makes it too hard to scoop and difficult to portion accurately.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Use cannabis-infused coconut cream instead of dairy for a vegan frozen treat with excellent THC binding properties.
Add fresh fruit puree to mask the herbal flavor while keeping the dosing consistent throughout.
Make popsicle molds for perfectly pre-portioned servings that eliminate the guesswork of scooping.

faq.q: Does freezing reduce the THC potency?
faq.a: No, freezing actually helps preserve THC by slowing the degradation process. Cannabinoids are stable at freezing temperatures and your frozen %{name} will retain potency for months. Light and heat are much bigger threats to potency than cold.

faq.q: Can I use cannabis tincture instead of infused fat?
faq.a: Yes, alcohol-based tinctures can work in frozen desserts. However, alcohol lowers the freezing point and may affect texture. Glycerin-based tinctures are a better alternative for frozen recipes as they blend more seamlessly.

faq.q: Why does my frozen edible taste too strongly of cannabis?
faq.a: Strong cannabis taste usually means the fat was not strained well enough, or you used too high a ratio of flower to fat during infusion. Double-strain through cheesecloth and consider adding vanilla, chocolate, or strong fruit flavors to balance it out.

faq.q: How long before a frozen edible takes effect?
faq.a: Like any edible, frozen treats can take up to 2 hours to kick in, because they still have to be digested. Always wait 2 hours before having more.

faq.q: Can I refreeze melted cannabis ice cream?
faq.a: You can refreeze it without losing THC potency, but the texture will suffer significantly with large ice crystals forming. If it has fully melted, consider repurposing it as a milkshake or sauce rather than refreezing.

confections.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe transforms %{base_fat} into an elegant, precisely dosed confection that looks as good as it tastes. Candies and confections are perfect for micro-dosing since each piece can be made to exact specifications. Master the art of cannabis candy making with our detailed guide.
dosing_tips: Confections are ideal for precise dosing because you can use molds to create identical portions. Calculate total THC and divide by the number of molds.
Mix the %{base_fat} in completely while the mixture is warm; in candies and gummies, a little sunflower lecithin helps it stay bound.
Make every piece the same size so each one carries the same dose. If you're new, start with about 5 mg, even if that's part of a piece, and wait 2 hours.
Allow confections to set completely before cutting, so every piece comes out the same size and the same dose.
common_mistakes: Heating sugar mixtures above 300 F (150 C) with cannabis fat already added will destroy a significant percentage of the THC. Add the infused fat after the candy reaches temperature and has cooled slightly.
Failing to use a candy thermometer leads to inconsistent results. Different candy stages (soft ball, hard crack) require precise temperatures.
Pouring the mixture too quickly into molds creates air bubbles that trap fat unevenly, leading to inconsistent dosing across pieces.
Not using molds or not using consistent mold sizes means each confection will have a different dose, making it impossible to control intake.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Add food-grade terpene flavorings that match your cannabis strain's aroma for a coordinated flavor profile.
Use silicone molds in fun shapes to make your confections more appealing and to ensure consistent sizing for accurate dosing.
Infuse white chocolate with cannabis oil for a milder-flavored confection that pairs well with fruit and nut additions.

faq.q: What is the best type of cannabis fat for making candy?
faq.a: Cannabis-infused coconut oil is the top choice for most confections because it solidifies at room temperature and has a neutral flavor. For chocolate-based confections, cannabis butter works beautifully. Both bind THC effectively and integrate smoothly into candy recipes.

faq.q: How do I prevent my cannabis chocolates from blooming?
faq.a: Bloom occurs when chocolate is not properly tempered. Heat your chocolate slowly, stir in the cannabis oil at the right temperature, then cool gradually. Using a double boiler and a thermometer keeps the process controlled and produces a professional shine.

faq.q: Why do my gummies have an oily layer on top?
faq.a: This happens when the cannabis fat does not emulsify with the gelatin mixture. Add a small amount of sunflower lecithin as an emulsifier, and stir continuously while the mixture is warm. Pouring into molds quickly before it begins to set also helps.

faq.q: How long do cannabis gummies last?
faq.a: It depends on what's in them, so follow the storage note for each recipe. Homemade gelatin gummies keep best sealed in the fridge, and freezing keeps them longer. THC stays stable as long as they're kept away from heat and light.

pastries.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe layers %{base_fat} into flaky, buttery pastry dough for an indulgent infused treat baked at %{cook_temp}. Pastries offer a sophisticated edible experience where the cannabis fat is an integral part of the dough structure. The lamination or folding process naturally distributes THC evenly throughout each layer.
dosing_tips: Calculate total THC in your %{base_fat} and divide by the number of pastries you plan to cut. Pastry dough distributes fat evenly through layering.
Keep doses moderate at 5-15 mg per pastry since these are rich foods that people tend to eat slowly, making onset timing unpredictable.
Weigh your dough portions on a kitchen scale to ensure each pastry has the same amount of infused fat.
Filled pastries can have cannabis in the dough, the filling, or both. Decide your strategy before starting and calculate accordingly.
common_mistakes: Working with warm dough causes the %{base_fat} to melt into the flour instead of staying in distinct layers, ruining both texture and THC distribution.
Overbaking at temperatures above %{cook_temp} for too long browns the butter and can degrade cannabinoids in the outer layers.
Rolling the dough too thin in some areas and thick in others creates uneven dosing between pastries from the same batch.
Skipping the resting periods between folds makes the dough tough and prevents proper layer formation.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Use cannabis-infused ghee for an even higher smoke point and nuttier flavor that works beautifully in puff pastry and croissants.
Fill with cannabis-infused pastry cream for a double-infused treat, but reduce the dough infusion to keep the total dose manageable.
Brush finished pastries with a cannabis honey glaze for an extra layer of flavor and a mild additional dose.

faq.q: Does the lamination process affect THC potency?
faq.a: No, lamination happens at cold temperatures which preserve THC. The folding actually helps distribute the cannabis fat more evenly throughout the dough. Just ensure you keep the dough cold and work quickly.

faq.q: Can I substitute cannabis oil for butter in pastry dough?
faq.a: Butter is strongly preferred for pastries because it creates the steam pockets that form flaky layers. If you must avoid dairy, cannabis-infused coconut oil in solid form is the closest substitute, though the texture will differ slightly.

faq.q: Why is my pastry dough greasy instead of flaky?
faq.a: Greasy dough means the fat melted during handling. Cannabis butter should be very cold and firm when incorporated. Work in a cool kitchen, chill the dough between folds, and handle it as little as possible. Cold fat equals flaky layers.

faq.q: How long do cannabis pastries take to kick in?
faq.a: Like any edible, pastries can take up to 2 hours to kick in, and a rich, buttery dough takes a while to digest. Eat one serving and wait at least 2 hours before having more.

faq.q: Can I use store-bought puff pastry and add cannabis?
faq.a: Yes, you can brush store-bought puff pastry sheets with melted %{base_fat} between layers, or use an infused filling. This is a great shortcut. Calculate the dose based on how much cannabis fat you add rather than what is in the dough.

puddings.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe infuses creamy custard with %{base_fat} for a smooth, comforting dessert that is simple to make and easy to dose. Puddings and custards are beginner-friendly edibles because the liquid base allows for thorough mixing and even THC distribution. Serve chilled for the best flavor and texture.
dosing_tips: Puddings are excellent for precise dosing because the liquid base mixes thoroughly. Stir continuously to ensure even distribution of %{base_fat}.
Pour into individual ramekins or cups for pre-portioned servings with a known dose per container.
New to edibles? Start with about 5 mg. A soft pudding goes down fast, but it can still take up to 2 hours to kick in.
If making a large batch, stir well before portioning since fat can rise to the top as the pudding cools.
common_mistakes: Boiling the custard mixture aggressively can curdle the eggs and break the emulsion, causing the cannabis fat to separate and pool on top.
Adding %{base_fat} to an already-set pudding means it will not incorporate. Always add it while the mixture is warm and liquid.
Not straining the custard base before chilling leaves lumps that can concentrate cannabis fat in certain bites.
Using too much cannabis fat changes the pudding's texture from creamy to greasy. Stick to the recipe's fat ratio and compensate by using more concentrated infusions.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Replace dairy milk with cannabis-infused coconut milk for a vegan version that has a natural affinity for binding cannabinoids.
Layer your cannabis pudding with non-infused whipped cream and crushed cookies for a parfait-style presentation.
Add a shot of espresso to chocolate cannabis pudding for a mocha flavor that complements and partially masks the herbal taste.

faq.q: Why did my cannabis pudding separate?
faq.a: Separation usually happens when the fat is not properly emulsified into the custard base. Whisk the %{base_fat} into the warm milk before adding other ingredients, and cook over medium-low heat while stirring constantly. Adding a pinch of lecithin also helps stabilize the emulsion.

faq.q: Can I use cannabis tincture instead of fat in pudding?
faq.a: Yes, alcohol-based tincture can be stirred into warm pudding and the alcohol will mostly evaporate. This produces a cleaner flavor with less herbal taste. Glycerin tinctures also work well and add a subtle sweetness.

faq.q: Do cannabis puddings hit faster than brownies?
faq.a: Don't count on it. A pudding is softer than a brownie, but any edible can take up to 2 hours to kick in, and timing varies a lot from person to person. Always wait 2 hours before taking more.

faq.q: How do I make the cannabis taste less noticeable in pudding?
faq.a: Strong flavors like chocolate, caramel, coffee, and citrus do the best job masking cannabis taste. Use well-strained, high-quality %{base_fat} and consider infusing at a lower flower-to-fat ratio for a longer time to extract cannabinoids without as much plant flavor.

faq.q: Can I heat cannabis pudding in the microwave?
faq.a: You can warm it gently but avoid overheating. Microwaving on high can create hot spots that degrade THC locally. Use 50% power in 15-second intervals, stirring between each. Honestly, most cannabis puddings taste best chilled or at room temperature.

custard.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe combines %{base_fat} with eggs and cream for a silky, rich custard that delivers a perfectly measured dose in every spoonful. Custards are an elegant way to enjoy cannabis edibles because the egg-and-fat base creates a natural emulsion that distributes THC with exceptional evenness. Baked gently at %{cook_temp}, your cannabis custard will set beautifully.
dosing_tips: Whisk %{base_fat} into the warm cream base before adding eggs to ensure the cannabis fat is fully emulsified throughout the custard.
Pour into individual ramekins for pre-portioned servings with a precise, known dose per cup.
If you're new, start with about 5 mg, part of a ramekin. Custards are rich and eaten slowly, so effects build gradually over 60-90 minutes.
Strain the custard mixture through a fine sieve before baking to remove any lumps and guarantee even THC distribution.
common_mistakes: Overheating the cream and %{base_fat} mixture causes the eggs to scramble when added, ruining the smooth texture and creating uneven THC pockets.
Cooking the custard too hot or too fast. Bake it in a water bath, or stir it over low heat, exactly as the recipe says; too much heat curdles the eggs and pushes the fat out.
Skipping the water bath when baking leads to overcooked edges and undercooked centers, meaning inconsistent potency across each serving.
Adding the cannabis fat directly to cold eggs instead of tempering slowly results in separation and a grainy finished custard.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Make a cannabis creme brulee by torching a thin sugar crust on top of your chilled cannabis custard for a dramatic presentation.
Infuse the cream with vanilla bean, lavender, or citrus zest alongside the %{base_fat} for a gourmet flavor profile.
Use cannabis coconut cream instead of dairy for a vegan custard set with agar rather than eggs.

faq.q: Why did my cannabis %{name} curdle in the oven?
faq.a: Curdling happens when custard is baked at too high a temperature or for too long. Always use a water bath at %{cook_temp} and check for doneness early. The center should jiggle slightly like gelatin when done. The cannabis fat does not cause curdling; it is purely a heat issue.

faq.q: Can I use cannabis cream instead of infused butter in custard?
faq.a: Yes, cannabis-infused cream is actually ideal for custard since cream is already a primary ingredient. This eliminates the need to emulsify a separate fat and produces the smoothest possible texture. Calculate your dose based on the potency of the infused cream.

faq.q: How long does a cannabis custard take to kick in?
faq.a: Expect 45-90 minutes for full onset. The high fat and protein content from eggs and cream creates a slow, steady digestion that typically produces gradual, long-lasting effects. This makes custard a forgiving edible format for managing your experience.

faq.q: Does the water bath affect THC potency?
faq.a: No, the water bath is essential and does not affect THC at all. It simply regulates the oven temperature around the custard, keeping it gentle and even. This indirect heat actually protects cannabinoids better than direct dry oven heat.

no_bake.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe needs no oven: the %{base_fat} is mixed into the other ingredients and the dessert sets as it chills. No-bake desserts are quick to make, and the one thing to get right for an even dose is the mixing.
dosing_tips: Mix the %{base_fat} in completely while the mixture is still soft, so every piece gets the same amount.
Spread or layer it evenly, then cut or portion it into the number of servings the recipe gives. Unequal pieces mean unequal doses.
Edibles can take up to 2 hours to kick in. Wait at least 2 hours before having more.
common_mistakes: Adding the %{base_fat} while it's very hot. Let melted fat cool slightly before it meets chocolate, cream or eggs, so nothing seizes, splits or scrambles.
Cutting before it has set. Chill it for the full time in the recipe, then cut with a sharp knife into clean, equal portions.
Forgetting it's medicated. Keep no-bake treats labelled and away from ordinary desserts.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Use the site's infused coconut oil instead of cannabutter for a dairy-free version, in the same amount so the dose stays the same.
Add a topping without cannabis (cocoa, fruit, nuts) to change the flavour without changing the dose.

faq.q: Can I use cannabis flower directly instead of an infused fat?
faq.a: No. Flower doesn't spread evenly through a no-bake dessert and makes it gritty. Make the infused fat first; the ingredient list links to it.

faq.q: Why does the cannabis still need to be decarboxylated if nothing is baked?
faq.a: Raw cannabis contains mostly THCA, which doesn't get you high until it's heated. The site's base recipes include that step, so the infused fat is ready to use.

faq.q: How do I make every piece the same dose?
faq.a: Mix thoroughly, press or layer the mixture to an even thickness, and cut it into exactly the number of servings the recipe doses for. Weighing the pieces is the most precise way.

stovetop.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe is cooked on the stovetop, not in the oven. The %{base_fat} goes into the batter or dough, or is brushed on at the end; it isn't used as the cooking or frying fat. Follow the steps for where the cannabis goes, and portion carefully for an even dose.
dosing_tips: Mix the %{base_fat} fully into the batter or dough before you start cooking, so every piece gets the same amount.
Use the same scoop or ladle for each piece and make exactly the number of servings the recipe doses for.
Edibles can take up to 2 hours to kick in. Wait at least 2 hours before having more.
common_mistakes: Cooking or frying in the infused fat itself. Use plain butter or oil in the pan or fryer, as the recipe says; the cannabis goes in the batter or on top.
Letting the batter sit without stirring. Fat can rise to the top, so stir before each pour or scoop.
Losing count because they taste like ordinary breakfast or street food. Keep track of how many servings you've had.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Make a dairy-free version with the site's infused coconut oil in place of cannabutter, in the same amount.
Serve with a topping without cannabis (fruit, syrup, sugar) to add flavour without adding THC.

faq.q: Can I fry in cannabis oil instead?
faq.a: It isn't a good idea: you'd need far more infused oil than the recipe doses, and you can't tell how much ends up in each piece. Fry in plain oil and keep the cannabis in the batter or on top, as written.

faq.q: Does cooking on the stove destroy the THC?
faq.a: Not at the times and temperatures in this recipe. The batter or dough stays much cooler inside than the pan or the oil, and the dose on this page already allows for some loss in cooking.

faq.q: Can I make them ahead?
faq.a: They're best fresh. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, follow the storage note above, and reheat them in a dry pan or the oven.

savory_snacks.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe uses %{base_fat} to create a savory, satisfying snack with precisely controlled THC content. Savory cannabis snacks are a welcome alternative to the sweetness of most edibles and pair beautifully with herbs and spices. The fat-soluble nature of THC makes savory applications with %{base_fat} a natural choice.
dosing_tips: Savory snacks are often eaten in handfuls, making portion control crucial. Pre-portion into individual servings of known dosage.
Drizzle or toss snacks with a measured amount of %{base_fat} rather than dipping, which leads to uneven coating and dosing.
When sharing, tell everyone how many mg one portion holds, and suggest that first-timers start with about 5 mg.
Spicy snacks can mask the cannabis taste and make you reach for more, so portion them out before you start eating.
common_mistakes: Cooking the snack too hot after the %{base_fat} is in. Use the temperature in the recipe, or add the %{base_fat} after cooking.
Unevenly coating items means some pieces are very potent while others have no cannabis. Toss in a bowl for even distribution.
Making a large bowl of snack mix without calculating per-serving doses leads to uncontrolled consumption.
Seasoning too lightly, thinking the cannabis adds flavor. Cannabis adds an herbal note, but you still need full seasoning.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Use cannabis-infused olive oil instead of butter for Mediterranean-style savory snacks like infused crackers or breadsticks.
Sprinkle nutritional yeast with finely ground decarbed kief for a cheesy seasoning that adds micro-doses to any snack.
Make a cannabis spice blend by mixing decarbed kief into your favorite seasoning mix for an easy sprinkle-on option.

faq.q: Do savory edibles hit differently than sweet ones?
faq.a: The onset and effects are similar regardless of flavor: what matters is how much THC is in a serving. The main advantage is variety and personal preference. Many people find savory edibles easier to dose-control because they are less tempting to overeat.

faq.q: What spices pair well with cannabis flavor?
faq.a: Herbs like rosemary, thyme, and oregano complement cannabis terpenes naturally. Garlic powder, smoked paprika, and cumin also work well. Bold spice profiles disguise the herbal cannabis notes while creating a complex, enjoyable flavor.

sweet_snacks.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe uses %{base_fat} to create a delightful sweet snack that delivers a reliable, enjoyable dose in every bite. Sweet snacks are the most popular category of cannabis edible for good reason, as sugar and fat together mask herbal flavors effectively. These no-fuss recipes are perfect for beginners and experienced consumers alike.
dosing_tips: Sweet snacks are the most likely edible to be overeaten. Pre-portion into individual packages with the dose written on each.
Mix %{base_fat} thoroughly into the warm sweet base before it sets to ensure each bite has an even amount of THC.
Bite-sized sweets make the dose easy to adjust: start with about 5 mg and wait 2 hours before eating more pieces.
Chocolate and caramel are excellent vehicles for cannabis because their strong flavors cover the herbal taste completely.
common_mistakes: Making treats that taste so good you forget they are medicated. Always be mindful of how many you have eaten and wait for effects.
Melting chocolate too hot before adding cannabis fat, which causes the mixture to seize and become grainy. Use gentle heat.
Not accounting for the calories in %{base_fat} when adding it to already sweet, rich recipes. The texture may become overly greasy.
Storing sweet snacks where children or pets could access them. Cannabis edibles must always be stored securely.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Drizzle cannabis-infused white chocolate over dried fruit and nuts for an elegant, easy-to-dose trail mix.
Use cannabis honey in granola bars or energy balls for a no-bake option that preserves full cannabinoid potency.
Roll no-bake cannabis truffles in cocoa powder, coconut flakes, or crushed nuts for variety in a single batch.

faq.q: Can I use cannabis sugar instead of fat in sweet snacks?
faq.a: Cannabis sugar can be made by evaporating a tincture onto granulated sugar. It works in recipes where the sugar dissolves, but the potency is typically lower and less consistent than fat-based infusions. It is best as a supplementary ingredient rather than the primary cannabis carrier.

faq.q: How do I make no-bake cannabis treats?
faq.a: Melt your %{base_fat} and mix it with ingredients like oats, nut butter, chocolate chips, and honey. Press into a pan or roll into balls, then refrigerate until set. No-bake methods preserve 100% of the THC since there is no heat exposure after decarboxylation.

faq.q: Are sweet edibles stronger than savory ones?
faq.a: No. A serving's strength depends on how much THC it holds, not on whether it is sweet or savory. The main difference is that sweet edibles are easier to overeat, leading to accidental overconsumption.

dips.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe blends %{base_fat} into a creamy, flavorful dip that is perfect for sharing at gatherings with informed guests. Cannabis dips are a versatile edible option that pairs with chips, vegetables, bread, and crackers. The creamy base naturally incorporates the infused fat for smooth, even dosing.
dosing_tips: Calculate the total THC in your batch and divide by the number of tablespoon-sized servings the recipe makes.
Serve with a designated spoon or portioning tool so guests know that one scoop equals one dose.
Provide a clearly marked card next to the dip stating the approximate mg per serving and recommending limits.
Mix the dip thoroughly since cannabis fat can settle or separate. Stir before each serving occasion.
common_mistakes: Not stirring the dip well enough causes the cannabis fat to pool in certain areas, giving some scoops ten times the dose of others.
Making dips too cannabis-forward in flavor. Bold ingredients like garlic, chipotle, herbs, and cheese easily mask the taste.
Putting cannabis dip out at a party without clear labeling. Everyone who might eat it must be informed and consenting.
Leaving the dip at room temperature too long. Dairy-based cannabis dips should be served cold and returned to the fridge after 2 hours.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Blend cannabis coconut oil into guacamole for a vegan-friendly infused dip where the avocado fat masks any oiliness.
Stir %{base_fat} into warm queso or cheese sauce for a potent, savory dip that stays emulsified thanks to the cheese.
Mix cannabis-infused olive oil with herbs, lemon, and yogurt for a Mediterranean-style dip.

faq.q: How do I prevent the cannabis taste in dips?
faq.a: Use strongly flavored bases like roasted garlic hummus, spicy bean dip, or pungent cheese spreads. These bold flavors dominate and mask the herbal cannabis notes. Well-strained, quality %{base_fat} also has less plant taste to begin with.

faq.q: Can I heat cannabis dip without losing potency?
faq.a: Gentle warming to serving temperature is fine. Keep it under 200 F (93 C) and you will preserve the THC. Avoid boiling or broiling cannabis dips. Warm them in a saucepan over low heat or in the microwave at reduced power.

faq.q: What is the best base for a cannabis dip?
faq.a: Cream cheese, sour cream, and avocado are excellent bases because they are already high in fat, which means the cannabis fat blends right in without changing the texture. Hummus and bean dips also work well with cannabis oil stirred in.

faq.q: How many servings should I plan per person?
faq.a: Limit it to one serving per person for newcomers and two for experienced consumers. Provide plenty of non-infused snacks alongside the cannabis dip so people are not tempted to overindulge. One to two tablespoons of dip per serving is typical.

faq.q: Can I use cannabis dip as a spread on sandwiches?
faq.a: Absolutely. A measured tablespoon of cannabis dip on a sandwich or wrap is a great way to dose consistently. This is especially convenient with cream cheese or hummus-based cannabis dips that spread easily and store well.

Savory bites are the ideal cannabis %{category} format because each piece is individually sized for a precise, consistent dose. These flavorful little bites pack bold seasoning that complements the herbal notes of cannabis.
dosing_tips: Calculate total THC in your %{base_fat} batch and divide by the exact number of bites you form for precise per-piece dosing.
Small bites make the dose easy to adjust: guests can start with about 5 mg and wait 2 hours before having another.
Use a small cookie scoop or tablespoon measure to ensure every bite is the same size and therefore the same dose.
Savory bites are snackable and easy to overeat. Set out a controlled number per person and store the rest.
common_mistakes: Forming bites of different sizes creates wildly different doses per piece. Weigh or measure each one consistently.
Baking savory bites at high temperatures to achieve crispness can degrade THC. Keep at or below %{cook_temp} and add %{base_fat} after baking if needed.
Under-seasoning savory bites lets the cannabis flavor dominate. Use garlic, herbs, cheese, and spices generously.
Leaving cannabis bites on a communal table without labeling. Always clearly indicate that they contain THC and state the dose per piece.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).

Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.

Stuff mushroom caps with a cannabis breadcrumb filling for a sophisticated, individually portioned savory bite.

faq.q: How many cannabis savory bites should I eat?
faq.a: Start with about 5 mg and wait 2 hours before having another bite. Savory bites are designed for easy portion control, but you must exercise discipline and track your intake.

faq.q: Can I make cannabis %{name} in advance for a party?
faq.a: Yes, most savory bites can be prepared a day ahead and refrigerated. Bring to room temperature or reheat gently before serving. Prepare a label card showing the THC content per piece and place it prominently next to the serving platter.

faq.q: What seasonings work best with cannabis savory bites?
faq.a: Bold flavors like smoked paprika, garlic powder, rosemary, parmesan, and everything bagel seasoning complement and mask cannabis notes. Umami-rich ingredients like sun-dried tomatoes and olives also pair exceptionally well.

faq.q: Are savory bites better than sweet edibles for dosing?
faq.a: Savory bites are excellent for dosing because they are less tempting to overeat than sweet treats. People tend to eat sweet edibles impulsively, while savory bites are consumed more mindfully. Both can be dosed precisely with proper preparation.

Serve with an array of dippers for a social, customizable experience.

Provide a serving spoon or small spatula so each person takes a consistent, measured amount.
Label the spread clearly with the approximate mg per tablespoon so consumers can make informed decisions.
Stir or remix the spread before each use, as cannabis fat can settle or migrate over time.

Create a cannabis compound butter with fresh herbs, garlic, and lemon zest for a versatile finishing spread.

faq.q: What is the best base for a cannabis spread?
faq.a: Cream cheese, nut butters, hummus, and softened butter are all excellent bases because they are already high in fat and thick enough to hold the cannabis oil in suspension. Choose based on your flavor preference and dietary needs.

faq.q: Can I buy store-bought spread and just add cannabis?
faq.a: Yes, stirring a measured amount of cannabis oil or melted cannabis butter into any store-bought spread is one of the easiest edible preparations. Mix thoroughly and recalculate the dose per serving based on what you added.

faq.q: How do I prevent the cannabis taste in my %{name}?
faq.a: Use well-strained, high-quality %{base_fat} and pair it with bold-flavored bases. Roasted garlic, chipotle, sun-dried tomato, and strong cheeses all overpower the herbal cannabis notes effectively.

faq.q: Can cannabis spreads be heated for dipping?
faq.a: Yes. Warm it gently to serving temperature, stirring often to keep it smooth, and don't let it boil.

faq.q: How do I serve cannabis spreads responsibly at a gathering?
faq.a: Place the cannabis spread on a separate, clearly marked section with a sign showing the dose per serving. Provide a dedicated serving utensil. Always have non-infused options available and only serve to informed, consenting adults.

finger_food.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe incorporates %{base_fat} into handheld, no-utensil-needed bites that make dosing social and fun. Cannabis finger foods are ideal for gatherings because each piece is self-contained with a known dose, eliminating the guesswork of shared dishes. Bold flavors and creative presentations make these %{category} options a hit.
dosing_tips: Make every piece the same size so each one carries the same dose, which keeps tracking straightforward.
Wrap, stuff, or encase the cannabis element inside the finger food so the THC is sealed in and evenly distributed.
Provide a tray card listing ingredients, allergens, and the exact THC dose per piece for responsible serving.
Finger foods are often eaten quickly in social settings. Remind guests that effects can take up to 2 hours, so they should wait that long before eating more.
common_mistakes: Making finger foods so small that the cannabis flavor is concentrated, or so large that people only eat half and get an inconsistent dose.
Applying %{base_fat} as an external glaze that rubs off on hands and napkins, reducing the actual consumed dose.
Cooking finger foods hotter or longer than the recipe says to crisp them up. If they need more colour, crisp them before the cannabis goes on, or add the cannabis at the end.
Forgetting to account for guests with dietary restrictions when choosing the finger food format.

Fill phyllo cups with cannabis cream cheese and smoked salmon for a sophisticated appetizer bite.
Skewer caprese salad components and drizzle with cannabis olive oil for a fresh, no-cook finger food option.

faq.q: How do I ensure even dosing in cannabis finger foods?
faq.a: The key is incorporating the %{base_fat} into a filling, spread, or dough that you then portion equally. Weigh each piece on a kitchen scale for consistency. Avoid drizzling cannabis oil on top, which leads to uneven distribution.

faq.q: How many cannabis finger foods should I serve per person?
faq.a: Check how many mg one piece holds: first-timers should stop at about 5 mg and wait 2 hours. Always provide ample non-infused finger foods alongside the cannabis options.

faq.q: Do cannabis finger foods work for micro-dosing?
faq.a: Finger foods are one of the best formats for micro-dosing. Make each piece contain 2.5 mg or less, allowing consumers to eat one and gauge effects before deciding on another. The small, controlled portions make it easy to fine-tune your experience.

fried_snacks.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe delivers crispy, golden perfection by strategically incorporating %{base_fat} without exposing it to destructive frying temperatures. Fried cannabis snacks require a specific technique: fry in regular oil for texture, then introduce the cannabis element through a finishing sauce, drizzle, or dipping component. This approach gives you the crunch you crave with full THC potency.
dosing_tips: Never fry directly in cannabis oil. Frying temperatures of 350-375 F (175-190 C) degrade THC rapidly. Add the cannabis component after frying.
Drizzle a measured amount of cannabis %{base_fat} over fried items immediately after draining, while they are still hot enough to absorb it.
Serve with a cannabis dipping sauce to control the dose precisely. Each tablespoon of sauce equals one measured dose.
Fried foods are calorie-dense and satisfying, which slows digestion. Expect onset in 60-90 minutes.
common_mistakes: Adding %{base_fat} to the deep fryer is the most common and most wasteful mistake. The high heat destroys THC and you lose the infused oil in the fryer.
Tossing fried snacks in too much cannabis oil makes them soggy instead of crispy. Use a light drizzle or mist.
Not draining fried items properly before adding cannabis oil, which traps steam and creates a greasy, limp texture.
Assuming a cannabis batter protects the THC during frying. Even batter-coated items reach internal temperatures that can degrade cannabinoids.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.

Create a cannabis aioli dipping sauce for fried snacks by blending cannabis oil into garlic mayo.
Drizzle cannabis honey over fried chicken strips or doughnut bites for a sweet-heat combination with precise dosing.

faq.q: What is the best cannabis dipping sauce for fried snacks?
faq.a: Cannabis ranch, cannabis garlic aioli, and cannabis honey mustard are all excellent options. The bold, creamy flavors mask cannabis taste, and each dip portion can be precisely measured for consistent dosing.

butter_oil.intro: This %{name} recipe is the foundation of all cannabis cooking: it shows you how to get maximum potency and clean flavor from your flower. Cannabis butter and oil are the building blocks that you will use in countless edible recipes. Master this essential technique and you will have consistent, reliable infusions every time.
dosing_tips: Calculate potency by multiplying the THC percentage of your flower by the weight in milligrams, then multiply by your expected extraction efficiency (typically 60-80%).
Label every batch with the date, strain, amount of flower used, and estimated mg per tablespoon for safe usage in recipes.
Start with a known strain from a licensed source so the THC percentage on the label gives you a reliable starting point for calculations.
Test a small amount of your finished infusion before cooking a whole recipe. Take about 5 mg worth (the page shows how much one teaspoon holds) and wait 2 hours to gauge potency.
common_mistakes: Skipping decarboxylation is the number one mistake. Raw cannabis contains THCA which is not psychoactive. Heat it at 240 F (115 C) for 40 minutes first.
Cooking the infusion at too high a temperature. Keep it at a gentle simmer, 160-200 F (70-93 C), never a rolling boil.
Not straining thoroughly. Squeeze the cheesecloth to get all the infused fat out, but do not force plant material through.
Changing the flower-to-fat ratio without updating the dose. Every recipe on this site assumes the base recipe's own ratio; if you use more or less flower, enter the new grams in the calculator.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Infuse coconut oil for a versatile, dairy-free option with excellent THC binding due to its high saturated fat content.
Make cannabis ghee by clarifying the butter after infusion. It has a higher smoke point and longer shelf life than regular cannabis butter.
Try infusing MCT oil for a neutral flavor that stays liquid at room temperature and works in any recipe.

faq.q: What is the best fat for cannabis infusion?
faq.a: Butter and coconut oil are the most common; olive oil works too. Pick the fat that suits what you'll cook; the dose depends on how much flower goes into each cup of fat, which each base recipe gives.

faq.q: How long should I cook the infusion?
faq.a: Low and slow is the key. Simmer at 160-200 F (70-93 C) for 2-4 hours on the stovetop, or 4-6 hours in a slow cooker on the low setting. Longer infusion times at low temperatures extract more cannabinoids without degrading them.

faq.q: Why is my cannabis butter green and bitter?
faq.a: Excessive green color and bitterness come from extracting chlorophyll and plant matter. Cook at lower temperatures, do not boil, and avoid grinding your flower too finely. A coarse grind with gentle heat produces a milder-tasting, golden butter.

faq.q: Do I need to add water when making cannabis butter?
faq.a: Adding water to the pot during infusion helps regulate temperature and prevents burning. The water separates from the butter when cooled in the fridge and can be drained off. This technique produces cleaner-tasting butter with fewer impurities.

faq.q: Can I make cannabis oil in a slow cooker?
faq.a: Yes, a slow cooker on the low setting is one of the best methods because it maintains a steady, low temperature for hours. Combine decarbed flower and oil, set to low, and let it go for 4-6 hours with occasional stirring. It is nearly foolproof.

milk_cream.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe infuses dairy with THC for a versatile ingredient that can be added to beverages, desserts, sauces, and more. Cannabis-infused milk and cream open up a world of culinary possibilities beyond traditional butter-based edibles. The milk fat naturally binds cannabinoids, and the liquid form makes measuring and mixing effortless.
dosing_tips: Use full-fat milk or heavy cream for maximum THC extraction. Skim milk does not have enough fat to bind cannabinoids effectively.
Measure doses by volume since liquid is easy to portion. Calculate the total mg in your batch and divide by the number of tablespoons or cups.
Add measured amounts to coffee, tea, or cereal for a controlled morning or evening dose.
Cannabis cream is more potent per volume than cannabis milk due to higher fat content. Adjust recipes accordingly.
common_mistakes: Using low-fat or skim milk results in very weak infusions because there is not enough fat to extract and hold the THC.
Boiling the milk scorches it and creates an unpleasant flavor while potentially degrading THC. Keep it at a gentle simmer below 180 F (82 C).
Not decarboxylating the flower first. Simmering in milk alone does not fully activate the THCA into THC.
Infusing for too short a time. Milk needs at least 45-60 minutes of gentle simmering to extract cannabinoids adequately.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).

Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Infuse heavy cream and whip it for a cannabis topping on desserts, hot chocolate, or coffee.
Use cannabis-infused coconut milk for a dairy-free alternative that has high fat content for good THC binding.
Make cannabis condensed milk by simmering infused milk with sugar until reduced, perfect for desserts and cocktails.

faq.q: Can I make cannabis milk with plant-based milk?
faq.a: Full-fat coconut milk works well because of its high fat content. Oat milk and almond milk have much less fat and will produce weaker infusions. If using low-fat plant milks, add a tablespoon of coconut oil to boost fat content and improve extraction.

faq.q: How strong is cannabis milk compared to cannabis butter?
faq.a: Cannabis milk is typically less potent per volume because milk has less fat than butter. A cup of cannabis butter might contain significantly more THC than a cup of cannabis milk. However, cannabis cream approaches butter levels. Adjust your recipe calculations accordingly.

faq.q: Can I add cannabis milk to hot coffee without losing THC?
faq.a: Yes, the temperature of hot coffee is well below the THC degradation point. Stirring cannabis milk or cream into hot beverages is one of the most popular and effective uses. The heat actually helps the fat dissolve smoothly into the drink.

faq.q: Why did my cannabis milk curdle?
faq.a: Curdling happens when milk overheats or when acid is introduced. Keep the temperature below 180 F (82 C) during infusion. If adding to coffee or acidic drinks, warm the cannabis milk first and add it slowly. Fresh milk is also less likely to curdle than older milk.

faq.q: How do I strain cannabis milk?
faq.a: Use a fine mesh strainer lined with cheesecloth. Pour the milk through slowly and gently squeeze the cheesecloth to extract all the liquid. For an extra-smooth result, strain twice. Do not press too hard or you will push plant matter through.

Start with about 5 mg (the page shows how much one teaspoon holds) in your coffee or tea and wait 2 hours to gauge potency before adding more next time.
Use a squeeze bottle or dropper for precise dispensing. Every drop should deliver a consistent, known amount of THC.
Cannabis sweeteners can be deceptively potent because they are concentrated. Always measure rather than free-pouring.
common_mistakes: Heating cannabis honey or syrup above 300 F (150 C) when cooking destroys THC. Add sweetener to finished dishes or use in no-heat applications.
Not stirring cannabis-infused honey thoroughly during preparation, which causes the cannabis to settle and creates inconsistent potency.
Making sweetener too thick or crystallized, which makes accurate measuring difficult. Maintain a pourable consistency.
Assuming cannabis sugar has the same potency as cannabis oil. Sugar-based infusions are typically less concentrated and less efficient.

faq.q: Can I use cannabis %{name} in baking?
faq.a: Yes, but only add it to recipes where the sweetener is not exposed to temperatures above 300 F (150 C) for extended periods. It works best in no-bake recipes, frostings, glazes, and beverages. For baked goods, add the cannabis sweetener after baking as a drizzle.

faq.q: How long does cannabis simple syrup last?
faq.a: Like any homemade syrup, keep it sealed in the fridge and use it within the time in the recipe's storage note. Freeze it in an ice-cube tray to keep it longer.

tincture.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe extracts potent cannabinoids into a liquid form that offers precise, sublingual dosing without any cooking required. Cannabis tinctures are one of the most important %{category} preparations because they are versatile, fast-acting when taken under the tongue, and can be added to virtually any food or drink. Master this technique for the ultimate cannabis pantry staple.
dosing_tips: Use a graduated dropper to measure each dose in milliliters. Calculate the total THC in your batch and divide by the total volume for mg-per-ml accuracy.
For sublingual use, hold the tincture under your tongue for 60-90 seconds before swallowing. Effects can onset in 15-30 minutes this way.
When adding tincture to food, effects follow normal edible timing of 45-90 minutes since it goes through digestion.
Start with about 5 mg, a fraction of one serving: tinctures are concentrated and easy to overdose.
common_mistakes: Using low-proof alcohol for extraction produces a weak tincture. Use 190-proof food-grade ethanol for maximum cannabinoid extraction.
Not decarboxylating the flower before soaking in alcohol. Raw cannabis in alcohol extracts THCA, which is not psychoactive.
Shaking or agitating the tincture too aggressively during extraction, which pulls out excessive chlorophyll and makes it bitter and green.
Storing tincture in a clear glass bottle where light degrades cannabinoids. Always use amber or cobalt blue glass.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Make a glycerin-based tincture for an alcohol-free option that is slightly sweet and gentler on the palate.
Create a fast-wash tincture by freezing both the alcohol and decarbed flower, then combining for a short 3-minute extraction to minimize chlorophyll.
Stir a measured dose into a drink or a spoonful of honey instead of taking it under the tongue.

faq.q: What is the difference between alcohol and glycerin tinctures?
faq.a: Alcohol tinctures are more potent because ethanol extracts cannabinoids more efficiently. They also have a longer shelf life. Glycerin tinctures are milder, slightly sweet, alcohol-free, and better for people who avoid alcohol, but they are less potent per volume.

faq.q: How long does a cannabis tincture take to make?
faq.a: The traditional method takes 2-4 weeks of soaking with daily shaking. The fast-freeze method takes only 3-5 minutes of active extraction. Both produce effective tinctures, though the long soak extracts a broader spectrum of compounds including more terpenes.

faq.q: Can I evaporate the alcohol from my tincture?
faq.a: It isn't safe to do at home: high-proof alcohol gives off flammable vapour even at room temperature, and heating it makes that worse. If you want no alcohol, make the site's infused coconut oil or honey instead.

faq.q: Why does my tincture taste so harsh?
faq.a: Harsh taste comes from long extraction times that pull out chlorophyll and plant waxes. Use the quick-wash method with frozen ingredients, strain through a coffee filter, and consider a brief winterization step in the freezer to remove waxes.

faq.q: How do I add tincture to food without losing potency?
faq.a: Add tincture to finished dishes, not during cooking. Stir it into sauces, dressings, and beverages after they have been removed from heat. The alcohol evaporates quickly when added to warm food, leaving the cannabinoids behind without affecting flavor significantly.

condiment.intro: This cannabis %{name} recipe infuses an everyday condiment with %{base_fat} for an effortless way to add a measured dose of THC to any meal. Cannabis condiments are the ultimate %{category} convenience because you prepare them once and use them for weeks, turning ordinary meals into edible experiences with a simple squeeze or spoonful.

Measure the condiment with a spoon rather than pouring, so you know how many servings you're having; about 5 mg is a first-time dose.
Shake or stir your cannabis condiment before each use since the infused fat can separate over time.
Track your condiment consumption throughout the day if using it on multiple meals to avoid accidental over-dosing.
common_mistakes: Mixing cannabis oil into a condiment that is predominantly water-based without an emulsifier, causing visible oil separation.
Heating cannabis ketchup, mustard, or hot sauce to high temperatures on the stove, which degrades THC. Add condiments at serving time.
Making a large batch with imprecise dosing math, resulting in condiments that are either too weak to feel or dangerously strong.
Storing cannabis condiments alongside regular ones without clear labeling, leading to accidental consumption by housemates.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Blend %{base_fat} into mayonnaise for a cannabis aioli that works on sandwiches, burgers, fries, and as a dipping sauce.
Stir cannabis oil into sriracha or your favorite hot sauce for a spicy, infused condiment that masks herbal flavors.
Make cannabis-infused pesto by blending %{base_fat} with basil, garlic, pine nuts, and parmesan for a versatile condiment.

faq.q: What condiments are easiest to infuse with cannabis?
faq.a: Oil-based and fat-based condiments are the easiest: mayonnaise, pesto, salad dressings, and butter-based sauces. They naturally incorporate cannabis fat without separation issues. Water-based condiments like ketchup and mustard require an emulsifier like lecithin.

faq.q: How do I dose cannabis condiments accurately?
faq.a: Calculate total THC in the batch, measure the total volume, and determine mg per tablespoon. Then use a measuring spoon each time you serve rather than squeezing freely. Consistency in measuring is the key to reliable dosing with condiments.

faq.q: Will cooking with cannabis condiments reduce THC?
faq.a: If you add the condiment to hot food at serving temperature, THC is preserved. If you cook or bake with it at high temperatures for extended periods, some THC will degrade. Use cannabis condiments as finishing additions rather than cooking ingredients.

faq.q: Can I take cannabis condiments to a barbecue?
faq.a: You can bring them for personal use, but never set them out without extremely clear labeling. Keep them in a separate, distinct container away from regular condiments. Only share with informed, consenting adults who understand the dose per serving.

dosing_tips: The page shows the mg in one level teaspoon; that teaspoon is one serving.
Use at most one teaspoon per serving of the dish you make, and make up the rest of the recipe with the plain ingredient.
Stir or shake the jar before measuring, so every spoonful holds the same share of the cannabis.
New to edibles? Start with about 5 mg, a third of a teaspoon, and wait 2 hours before having more.
common_mistakes: Swapping it one-for-one for the plain ingredient. A whole cup holds dozens of servings.
Measuring heaped spoons. Level each teaspoon with a knife so the dose matches the page.
Skipping the decarb. Raw flower is mostly THCA, which has no effect; this recipe heats it in the oven first.
Letting it get damp. Moisture makes it clump, and clumps make the dose in each spoonful uneven; keep the jar sealed and dry.
storage: Follow the storage note at the end of this list. Anything made with dairy, eggs, cream cheese, meat or fish goes into the fridge within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour above 90°F / 32°C).
If the recipe freezes well, freeze single, labelled portions so you can thaw one dose at a time.
Label every container with the date and the mg per serving, and keep edibles out of reach of children and pets.
variations: Use it in a recipe with a known number of servings, one level teaspoon per serving, so the calculator's dose stays right.
Whisk the measured amount into the rest of the dry ingredients first, so it spreads evenly through the dough or batter.

faq.q: Can I use %{name} in place of all the plain ingredient?
faq.a: No. One level teaspoon is one serving, so a whole cup holds dozens of servings. Use one teaspoon per serving and the plain ingredient for the rest.

faq.q: Can I eat cannabis flour raw?
